whenApp.label: Use Cases
whenApp.title: When Is a Dedicated App Worth It?
whenApp.description: An app isn't automatically the best solution for every digital project. It becomes especially interesting when users interact with a product regularly, or when features are needed that go beyond a classic website.

items.title: Regular Usage
items.description: Fast access directly from the smartphone and a more product-focused user experience.

items.title: Push Notifications
items.description: Proactively inform users about new content, reminders or relevant events.

items.title: Offline Functionality
items.description: Make certain features and data available even without a permanent internet connection.

items.title: Device Features
items.description: Integrate camera, GPS or other smartphone features into the product.

items.title: User Accounts
items.description: Enable personalized content, individual data and recurring usage.

items.title: Complex Workflows
items.description: Structure mobile processes that go beyond a simple website.

items.title: App Store Presence
items.description: Make a digital product available as a standalone application via the Apple App Store and Google Play.

whenApp.note: If a web app or responsive website makes more sense for a project, that should be part of the consultation too. I don't automatically recommend an app, but the technically and economically most sensible approach.

appVsWebApp.label: Decision Guide
appVsWebApp.title: Mobile App or Web App – What Fits the Project?

mobileApp.title: Mobile App
items: Installation via App Store / Google Play

webApp.title: Web App
items: Updates can be rolled out directly
Often a lower barrier to entry
Useful for browser-based applications and internal tools

appVsWebApp.note: Which variant makes more sense depends on user behavior, required features, budget and long-term product goals.

mvp.label: MVP Approach
mvp.title: Validate First, Then Expand Strategically
mvp.description: For new product ideas, not every planned feature needs to be built right away. An MVP focuses on the most important features that let the product be used and tested for real, for the first time.
mvp.note: The goal isn't to build as little as possible, but to build the features that are decisive for real-world use first.

faq.label: FAQ
faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions About App Development

items.question: What does it cost to build an app?
items.answer: Costs depend heavily on feature scope, design, backend, integrations and technical requirements. After an initial consultation, the required scope can be structured and a realistic effort estimate created.

items.question: How long does it take to build an app?
items.answer: That depends on the scope. A focused MVP can be built much faster than a complex platform with backend, user accounts and numerous integrations. A realistic project scope and timeline is defined at the start.

items.question: Do you develop apps for iOS and Android?
items.answer: Yes. For many projects I work with Flutter, which lets me build iOS and Android applications from a shared codebase.

items.question: Do I need two different apps for iOS and Android?
items.answer: Not necessarily. With cross-platform technologies like Flutter, a large part of the application can be built together. Platform-specific adjustments may still be necessary.

items.question: What is Flutter?
items.answer: Flutter is a framework for building applications for multiple platforms from a shared codebase. I use Flutter especially for iOS and Android projects.

items.question: Do you also build MVPs?
items.answer: Yes. For new product ideas, a focused first version with the most important features can be built first. The product can then be expanded strategically based on real usage and feedback.

items.question: Can you develop existing apps further?
items.answer: Yes. Existing applications can also be developed further through new features, bug fixes, integrations or design updates.

items.question: Can you implement existing Figma designs?
items.answer: Yes. Existing Figma screens can be technically implemented as design-to-code and integrated into an existing or new app.

items.question: Do you support App Store and Google Play releases?
items.answer: Yes. Publishing can be considered and technically prepared as part of the project.

items.question: Do I even need an app for my idea?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Depending on usage, features and budget, a responsive website or web app may make more sense. This decision should be clarified before development begins.

items.question: Can an app also work offline?
items.answer: Yes. Depending on the use case, data can be stored locally and certain features used even without a permanent internet connection. Pictolog PDF, for example, is designed as an offline application.
